chapter: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
title: Learning to be a Negro: signs, caution and survival
summary: Growing up in the South meant reading segregation signs and learning caution; Danny says survival depended on being alert.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: But you see, because a Black has to... When you're a Negro in America, you have to learn to be a Negro. You have to go through a schooling. You don't know. And you constantly shop, but you can't do this and you can't do that. And in the case of New Orleans and the South, you had to learn to read the signs right away. White Men's Room, White Gentleman's Bath, Negro Man, White Ladies Dressing Room or Toilet or Black Women's Toilet.

It was always a putdown. So you're raised with a putdown from the beginning. So if your skin ain't tough, you're in trouble. You have to be watching all these.. You spend half of your time seeing can you go in somewhere. And you've got the money, the same as everybody else, but you've got to watch with this caution to keep out of trouble. Because any bum, a White bum, no matter if he's a wino, he

can holler, "What are you doin' in here, you?! Make him get out of here!" The lowest bum you probably can find. It was his prerogative because he was White. So you had to learn how to roll with the punches, and all them scars is on your personality. If you're smart and listen to what older people tell you, then you learn how to survive.
So that's what you had here in New Orleans, a multi...a triple multi-level society.

And the Black was the lowest upon the totem pole, the last run. So for you to survive, you had to be very alert, you know... Watch them seven holes in your head. I got some kids, I'll be teaching them. I'll ask them, "How many holes you got in your head?" They don't know what the hell I'm talking about. I ask them, "How many holes...?" They say, "One, two..." But there are seven. One, two, two eyes; two nostrils...

And your mouth and your two ears. So you've got to keep that in coordination at all times. In fact, I did... Today they have all kind of openings for them. They don't see no signs. They don't know what it was to have a sign on a bus or on a streetcar. And you had to maneuver to
put the sign in front of yourself. That's the way it was rigged up.
